author: Mo Qureshi
headline: Saudi transport ministry and DHL join Riyadh logistics summit panels
deck: The summit's panel composition covered the regulator, the shippers, the operators and the investors — the four positions in the argument.
excerpt: The Saudi logistics summit drew panels from the transport ministry, the Federation of Saudi Chambers, DHL Global Forwarding, Morph Logistics and Caden Investment.
content:
A summit ran alongside the Saudi Warehousing and Logistics Expo at Riyadh's convention centre on its opening day, with panels drawn from the Ministry of Transport and Logistic Services, the Federation of Saudi Chambers, DHL Global Forwarding Saudi Arabia, Morph Logistics Solutions and Caden Investment.

The composition is worth reading, because those five organisations occupy the four distinct positions in any logistics market argument.

The ministry sets the terms. It licenses operators, designates logistics zones and determines the conditions under which foreign operators may hold Saudi warehousing and distribution assets. Everything the other parties do happens within that framework.

The Federation of Saudi Chambers represents the shippers — the manufacturers, traders and distributors who buy logistics services rather than sell them. Their interest is cost, reliability and coverage, and they are the demand side of the market the rest of the room serves.

DHL Global Forwarding brings the international contract logistics position, arguing a case this publication has examined separately: that Saudi manufacturers currently running their own distribution fleets would gain from outsourcing to operators who can run the same assets at higher utilisation across multiple customers.

Morph Logistics Solutions and Caden Investment supply the domestic operator and investor perspectives. The investor position is the one most often missing from these discussions and the most consequential, since logistics capacity is capital-intensive and someone has to fund the warehouses, fleets and handling equipment before the demand materialises.

The declared agenda covered infrastructure and investment, multimodal connectivity, warehousing and distribution, digital resilience, supply chain security and trade facilitation — six themes that map onto the same set of interests.

The market figures circulating at the exhibition came from the organiser rather than from the panels: a $6.7bn Saudi commercial vehicle market, e-commerce logistics projected to double by 2027, and 25 of 42 planned logistics hubs operational. This publication has examined that last figure separately, since the hubs still to come carry the harder infrastructure.

The exhibition itself drew more than 350 exhibiting companies from over 25 countries showing upwards of 4,000 products and services, as stated at its opening by Dr Rumaih bin Mohammed Al-Rumaih, Vice Minister of Transport and Logistic Services.

Panel participation is as reported from the opening day; session content and individual speaker detail are published by the organiser following the event.

Ministerial patronage at an exhibition in this sector carries practical weight, since the ministry in question licenses logistics operators and designates the zones within which they work. Exhibitors read its presence as a signal about policy direction.
